paragraphs.heading: The place and its size
paragraphs.text: Harappa was an ancient settlement in Punjab, Pakistan, about 24 kilometres west of Sahiwal. It takes its name from a modern village near the old course of the Ravi River, which now flows eight kilometres to the north. At its largest, in the Mature Harappan phase from 2600 to 1900 BC, the city is believed to have held as many as 23,500 people, with clay brick houses spread over about 150 hectares. That counts as large for its time. Today's village, less than a kilometre from the ruins, is a small crossroads town of 15,000 people.

paragraphs.heading: The site that named a civilisation
paragraphs.text: Harappa is the type site of the Indus Valley Civilisation. It was the first site of that culture excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India under British rule, and for this reason the whole civilisation is sometimes called Harappan. Its importance only became clear some years later, when Mohenjo-daro in Sindh was found. These two were the greatest cities of the civilisation, and both rose along the Indus valley. Their discovery crowned work that had begun when the Archaeological Survey of India was founded in 1861.

paragraphs.heading: Trade and daily life
paragraphs.text: The Indus people lived in an urban culture kept going by surplus farm produce and by commerce. Their weights and measures were highly standardised, following a fixed scale of steps. Distinctive seals were used, perhaps to mark property and goods being shipped. They used copper and bronze but not yet iron, wove and dyed cotton, grew wheat, rice, vegetables and fruit, and kept animals such as the humped bull. Trade routes along the Indus reached as far as the Persian Gulf, Mesopotamia and Egypt, with carnelian and lapis lazuli among the most valuable goods. Merchants also traded widely with people in southern India, near today's Karnataka, to obtain gold and copper.

paragraphs.heading: A slow decline
paragraphs.text: From around 2000 BC the cities slowly fell apart, in a stage lasting until 1300 BC that is called Late Harappan. Nothing suggests that invaders destroyed them; the evidence points strongly to natural causes. Studies show that today.s Thar Desert used to be much wetter, and that its climate dried out bit by bit. Falling sea levels led people to leave some regions, and in its later stages the civilisation lost features such as writing and water engineering. As a result, settlement in the Ganges Valley grew in importance.

paragraphs.heading: What the bones show
paragraphs.text: Skeletons from Harappa show a high rate of injury, 15.5%, especially in remains linked to the later phases. They often bear wounds that were likely made in battle. Leprosy and tuberculosis were both present, with the most disease and injury in skeletons from Area G, an ossuary south-east of the city walls. The rise in head and face injuries and infection seems to match the time when society declined. This hints that violence and disease mostly came after the collapse began, perhaps from social stress, scarce resources and people being shut out of basic health and safety.

paragraphs.heading: Damage and protection
paragraphs.text: The ruins were badly damaged under British rule. In 1857 engineers building the Lahore–Multan railway took bricks from the site to use as track ballast. Even so, a wealth of artefacts has been recovered. In 2004 UNESCO put Harappa on its tentative list for World Heritage Sites. A year later a disputed plan to build an amusement park there was dropped after builders dug up many artefacts in the early stages of work.
